title: Kill your own business
hook: Your DVD business is booming. Do you bet on streaming?

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Netflix is for what comes next

intro.text: It is 2000. You run Netflix, a small company that rents DVDs by post. You are losing money. Meanwhile Blockbuster, the giant of movie rental, earns about $800 million a year from late fees alone.

d1.title: Sell to the giant?
d1.setup: Money is tight. Blockbuster has stores everywhere and cash to spare. You could ask them to buy you and run their online rental for them.
d1.question: What do you do?
d1.advisor: There is no shame in looking for a safe harbour. Just don't give up on what you are building.

options.label: Offer to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million.
options.outcome: The founders offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster said no. Netflix kept growing its flat monthly fee and no-late-fee service, and reached 1 million subscribers within about three years.
options.why: Looking for a buyer was a sensible hedge for a small company losing money. But it could have handed your idea to a company that did not believe in it.
options.better: Raise money from investors who believe in the idea, and keep control of what you are building.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you tried to sell. Luckily the giant said no, and you kept your future.

options.label: Cut back to a tiny team and wait for better times.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you survive, but slowly. While you wait, others start renting DVDs online too.
options.why: Shrinking a young company saves money but stops the learning that makes it valuable.
options.better: Keep building, and raise money from people who believe in the idea.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you shrank when you should have kept learning.

options.label: Stay independent and raise money from investors who believe in it.
options.outcome: Our estimate: raising money is hard in a bad year, but you keep control. You keep growing the no-late-fee service that customers love.
options.why: You protected the thing that made you special, a model customers loved, instead of handing it to a rival.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you kept control of a model customers loved.

scene2006.text: It is 2006. Netflix went public in 2002, with over 500,000 subscribers, a $19.95 monthly plan and no late fees. Blockbuster launched its own online service in 2004, and now it lets members return DVDs in its stores. By the end of 2006 you have 6 million subscribers.

d2.title: Start streaming?
d2.setup: Your DVD business is strong, with more than 70,000 titles to choose from. Internet speeds are getting better, but watching movies online is still new and clumsy.
d2.question: What do you do about streaming?
d2.advisor: The DVD business is paying the bills. The question is how long it will keep doing that.

options.label: Wait until internet speeds are better. DVDs are doing fine.
options.outcome: Our estimate: profits look good for a few years, but when streaming takes off, others are ready and you are not.
options.why: Waiting for a technology to be perfect means a rival learns it first.
options.better: Start streaming now, even small, and learn while the DVD business pays the bills.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you waited for the future to be ready instead of getting ready for it.

options.label: Launch streaming as a paid extra on top of DVD plans.
options.outcome: Our estimate: a few keen fans pay extra, but most members never try it, so you learn slowly.
options.why: Charging for something new and clumsy keeps most people from trying it.
options.better: Give streaming away free inside existing plans so every member tries it.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you charged for the future before people knew they wanted it.

options.label: Add streaming free inside every plan.
options.outcome: In January 2007 Netflix added instant streaming on computers at no extra charge, with about 1,000 titles. How many hours you could watch depended on your plan.
options.why: Making streaming free meant every member tried it. You started moving customers to the future while the DVD business still paid the bills.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you gave the future away free so every customer would try it.

scene2010.text: It is 2010. Blockbuster has gone bankrupt, and Netflix has 20 million subscribers. In November you added a $7.99 streaming-only plan and raised the price of DVD plans. Netflix made $160 million in profit this year.

d3.title: Make your own shows?

setup.text: Streaming is taking off and you are behind. Every show you offer belongs to someone else, and they can take it away.
Almost everything you stream belongs to movie studios and TV networks. They can raise their prices or take shows away. A new political drama is looking for a home.

d3.question: Do you start paying for your own shows?
d3.advisor: TV networks usually test a pilot first. You do not have to play by their rules.

options.label: Keep licensing other people's shows. It is cheaper.
options.outcome: Our estimate: costs stay low for a while, but studios raise prices each year and keep their best shows for their own services.
options.why: If everything you sell belongs to someone else, they decide your future.
options.better: Own some of your shows, so you have something no one can take away.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you stayed dependent on suppliers who would one day be rivals.

options.label: Order a pilot episode first, like TV networks do.
options.outcome: Our estimate: you play it safe, but the show's makers want a full commitment, and a TV network wins the deal.
options.why: Playing by the old rules made you an ordinary bidder. Bold makers want a partner who commits.
options.better: Commit to a full series without a pilot and win the show.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you played by the old rules and lost a show that wanted a bold partner.

options.label: Outbid the TV networks and order two full seasons, with no pilot.
options.outcome: In March 2011 Netflix outbid HBO and AMC for a new drama called House of Cards and ordered two seasons, 26 episodes, without a pilot. The show would not be ready for almost two years.
options.why: You made a big bet on owning something no one else could offer, and you won it by committing more than the old players would.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you bought your way out of depending on suppliers.

d4.title: Split the price
d4.setup: It is July 2011. Your stock is near its highest ever, close to $304 a share. You want to push members toward streaming and buy more shows to stream. Members who want both DVDs and streaming pay about $10 a month.
d4.question: How do you change your plans?
d4.advisor: Members will forgive a change they understand. They hate a surprise in their bill.

options.label: Keep one plan and raise the price a little, with plenty of notice.
options.outcome: Our estimate: a few members grumble, but most stay. You get more money for new shows without a shock.
options.why: Small, well-explained changes keep trust while still moving the business forward.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you changed prices slowly and kept your members' trust.

options.label: Split DVDs and streaming into two plans at $7.99 each.
options.outcome: Netflix made DVDs and streaming separate plans at $7.99 each. Members who wanted both now paid about $16 instead of about $10. Many were angry, and in September Netflix lowered its forecast of how many subscribers it would have.
options.why: A 60% price rise all at once felt like a betrayal to loyal members.
options.better: Raise prices slowly and explain why, so members feel part of the change instead of punished by it.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you shocked loyal members with a big price rise all at once.

options.label: Stop DVDs completely and go streaming-only.
options.outcome: Our estimate: many members who still love DVDs leave, and you lose money you need for new shows.
options.why: The direction was right, but cutting off a business customers still used was too fast.
options.better: Keep DVDs while they still earn money, and move people to streaming with price and better shows.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you moved to the future faster than your customers could.

d5.title: After the backlash

setup.text: It is September 2011. Members are cancelling and your stock is falling. You think the plan is right, but people feel ignored.
It is September 2011. You want DVDs and streaming to be two different businesses, each with its own focus.

d5.question: What do you do with the DVD business?
d5.advisor: When customers are angry, ask first what they actually need from you.

options.label: Say sorry, and move DVDs to a new company with its own name and website.
options.outcome: Netflix's CEO apologized for poor communication and said DVDs would move to a new brand called Qwikster, with its own website. People mocked the name, and by October Netflix shares had lost more than half their value since July.
options.why: Members asked for one simple service. You gave them two websites and two bills, right when they were already upset.
options.better: Listen first: keep one website and one account, and explain clearly why prices changed.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you answered angry customers with more complexity.

options.label: Keep one website and one account, and explain the change clearly.
options.outcome: Our estimate: the anger cools down. Some members leave, but most stay, because the service still feels simple.
options.why: When trust is hurt, simple and honest beats clever.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you kept things simple when trust was at its lowest.

options.label: Undo everything and go back to the old prices.
options.outcome: Our estimate: members calm down, but you lose the money you needed for new shows, and investors wonder if you have a plan.
options.why: Rolling everything back fixes the anger but gives up a strategy that was right in direction.
options.better: Keep the strategy, fix how it was done: one account, clear communication.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you gave up a good plan because it was done badly.

d6.title: One last chance to fix it
d6.setup: It is October 2011. Everyone is laughing at the name Qwikster, and your stock keeps falling. You have weeks, not months.
d6.question: What now?
d6.advisor: Admitting a mistake fast is cheaper than defending it slowly.

options.label: Push ahead. Two companies is the right long-term plan.
options.outcome: Our estimate: more members leave, and the fight distracts everyone from building the streaming service.
options.why: Defending a mistake because you announced it only makes it bigger.
options.better: Drop the part customers hated quickly, and keep the part that serves the long-term plan.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you defended a mistake instead of fixing it.

options.label: Drop the separate DVD company, but keep the new prices.
options.outcome: Within weeks Netflix dropped Qwikster and kept one website and one account, but kept the new prices. In the July to September quarter its US subscribers had fallen from 24.6 million to 23.8 million, and Netflix said the price rise had hurt more than the name.
options.why: Backing down fast on the confusing part was smart. Keeping the prices gave you money for new shows, but cost you members.
options.better: Fix the mistake quickly, and pair the higher price with something members can see, like new shows.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you fixed the confusing part fast but kept the painful part.

options.label: Drop the DVD company and lower prices again for loyal members.
options.outcome: Our estimate: loyal members feel heard and come back. You have less money for shows this year, but trust is restored.
options.why: You fixed both the confusion and the shock, and showed members their loyalty mattered.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you won back trust by fixing both mistakes.

text.text: On February 1, 2013, Netflix released all 13 episodes of House of Cards on the same day. That quarter it added 2 million US streaming members, reaching 29.2 million, and its shares jumped 24% after the results.
Our estimate: you moved early to streaming and kept your members' trust. Netflix becomes the place people go to watch.

survivor.title: Bruised but alive
survivor.text: Our estimate: Netflix survives the storm, but rivals have caught up, and you spend years winning back what you lost.

collapse.title: The next Blockbuster
collapse.text: Our estimate: you waited too long or lost your members' trust. A rival becomes the home of streaming, and Netflix fades like the company it once beat.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Our estimate: after three costly calls in a row, the board loses its trust in you and asks someone else to lead Netflix.

realHistory: In 2000 Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster said no. In 2007 Netflix added streaming free to its DVD plans. In 2011 it ordered House of Cards without a pilot, then raised the price of DVDs plus streaming from about $10 to $16 and announced Qwikster, losing members and over half its stock value. It dropped Qwikster within weeks but kept the prices, and House of Cards helped it grow again in 2013.
